progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b03: a vector is a living carrier (a mosquito or tick) that takes a pathogen between hosts; Plasmodium develops inside Anopheles; "bed nets, repellent, and draining standing water where mosquitoes breed"; attempt 1 used draining and larvicide for Ross River virus. From b10: environmental management changes places so pathogens can't reach new hosts; the control board; evaluating by which link, how fast, how long and cost. From b11: "the drug selects resistance; it doesn't create it". From bio-m6-b01: selection raises the frequency of an existing resistance allele. From bio-m6-b18: an inserted gene from another source (recombinant DNA) can be expressed in a host. From bio-m6-b11 (flagged above): a gene drive copies itself to the partner chromosome so nearly all offspring inherit it; it has not been released in the wild. Not assumed: the Aedes life cycle, container breeding, larvicides, insecticide modes of action, day against night biting, the sterile insect technique, self-limiting males, Wolbachia, cytoplasmic incompatibility.
progression.startsWith: Follow a vector life cycle and environmental intervention. The video opens: In the 1950s, the world sprayed DDT to wipe out malaria, and within years, many mosquitoes could survive it.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining that a mosquito passes dengue on only if it bites an infected person, survives while the virus multiplies and bites again, so infection falls with fewer mosquitoes, fewer bites or mosquitoes that rarely pass the virus on; describing the *Aedes aegypti* life cycle (eggs above the waterline in containers, surviving dry months; larvae and pupae in water; adults in about a week; only females bite); explaining environmental management by removing breeding water and why it needs nearly every household (public health campaigns); explaining larvicides and adult sprays (insecticides that attack insect nerves) and why bed nets suit mostly night-biting *Anopheles* while indoor spraying of resting sites works against both (in Queensland, against day-biting *Aedes* in dengue outbreaks); explaining insecticide resistance by selection and the harm of sprays (other insects; DDT building up in food chains and thinning raptor eggshells); explaining the sterile insect technique and why releases must continue; explaining self-limiting genetically engineered males and recalling why gene drives are hard to reverse; explaining that Wolbachia isn't genetic engineering, blocks dengue in the mosquito and spreads by itself (passed through eggs; infected females' eggs hatch whichever male they mate with; eggs of uninfected females mated by infected males don't hatch); evaluating each method by how much it cuts transmission, how long it lasts, cost and harm, and justifying combined methods.
progression.nextLesson: what limits malaria and dengue control in practice (route entry bio-m7-b13).

teaching.task: In the 1950s, spraying DDT on mosquitoes bred resistance. In 2014, Townsville released more mosquitoes, and local dengue stayed rare for about ten years. How can controlling a vector reduce infection, and how do you judge which method to use?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why vector control cuts infection (transmission needs a bite, survival and a second bite; 2); why removing water works and fails (no water, no larvae; one missed container keeps breeding; 3, 4); why the method depends on biting time (nets only work when people are under them; 5); why sprays stop working (selection; 6); why sprays harm more than mosquitoes (broad action; build-up along food chains; 6); why sterile males cut numbers and why releases must continue (no offspring either way; 7); why self-limiting males cut biting females (daughters die; 8); why gene drives are risky (spread by themselves; 8); why Wolbachia spreads and lasts (passed through eggs; failed eggs for uninfected females; 9); why programs combine methods (each has a gap; 10). Visible case: the same wheel gains a break mark at the stage each method attacks; the same population row thins or turns teal. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; scenes 5 (pesticides and biting times) and 9 (Wolbachia's two pairings) are the densest, so earlier tags dim.
teaching.conversationalApproach: In the 1950s the world sprayed DDT to wipe out malaria and within years many mosquitoes could survive it, while in 2014 Townsville released more mosquitoes and local dengue stayed rare for about ten years, so the question is how controlling a vector reduces infection and how to judge which method to use. A vector is a living carrier, and Aedes aegypti carries dengue, so there are three ways to cut the link: fewer mosquitoes, fewer bites, or mosquitoes that rarely pass it on. The life cycle in a container of water shows the simplest control, taking away the water through public health campaigns. Pesticides kill larvae and adults, and timing matters because Aedes bites in the day, but insecticides select resistance alleles each generation and can harm other species. Sterile males reared and released leave no offspring, engineered males carry a gene that kills their female offspring, and gene drives could spread a gene through a population. Wolbachia is a natural bacterium, not genetic engineering, that blocks dengue inside the mosquito and passes from mothers to offspring, so the mosquitoes stay but dengue is blocked. Methods are judged by how much they cut transmission, how long the effect lasts, what they cost and what else they harm, and the memory aid is fewer mosquitoes, fewer bites, or mosquitoes that rarely pass it on. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: In the 1950s, the world sprayed DDT to wipe out malaria, and within years, many mosquitoes could survive it. In 2014, Townsville tried something that sounds backwards. It released more mosquitoes, carrying a bacterium. After the bacterium spread through the city's mosquitoes, local dengue stayed rare for about ten years. So how does controlling a vector cut infection, and why did adding mosquitoes help?

design.visualSystem: One mosquito life cycle wheel, drawn in scene 3 and kept at the left from then on: four stations round a circle, "eggs on a container wall", "larvae in water", "pupae", "adult female bites", each with its painted plate. Each method then lands on the wheel at the stage it attacks, as a coded `BreakMark` (b03's) with a small plate or chip: environmental management at "larvae in water" (the container tips), larvicide at "larvae", adult spray at "adult", bed nets at "bites" (for Anopheles, shown as a small second wheel thumbnail), sterile males at "eggs" (eggs don't hatch), self-limiting males at "larvae to adult" (daughters die), Wolbachia at "bites" (the virus is blocked, the mosquito lives). A coded population counter (a row of small Aedes glyph outlines that thins or refills) sits under the wheel in scenes 7 to 9. Wolbachia is a coded teal dot inside a mosquito glyph, explained once with the new painted `m7-wolbachia-cell-v1.png`. Scene 6 uses a coded survival bar across three generations and the aligned eggshell pair. Scene 10 is a coded four-column criteria table, b10's `CriteriaTable` re-used. No people, hands or faces: no households, sprayer operators, sleepers under nets, residents or scientists; the bed net plate (`m7-bed-net-v1.png`) is an empty bed; the sprayer is a plate without an operator; Townsville is a coded coastline outline with a dot. Scale: the mosquito, the larva and pupa plate, the container, the eggshell pair and the Wolbachia cell are never shown at one scale; each has its own grey label, and the Wolbachia cell carries "drawn far larger than real". Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides small grey labels; earlier chips dim to grey. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched (the container may rotate when it tips, never squash).
